st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied material contains only bibliography entries and provides no substantive argument, findings or recommendations about benchmark validity, reproducibility, governance or workplace suitability. A cited title on medical-oncology examination performance is benchmark-adjacent, but it does not reveal the source’s position on whether high scores establish reliable professional performance.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied material consists only of bibliography entries and does not reveal the source’s own position on whether credible AI evaluation must test realistic professional task execution or how such tasks should be scored and validated. One cited title calls for creative-task benchmarks, but citation alone does not establish endorsement or a developed evaluation argument.
qs: Societal impacts research requires benchmarks for creative   composition tasks.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between AI-assisted productivity and durable skill formation, then materially extends it by identifying independent error resolution, cognitive effort and conceptual engagement as interaction patterns associated with better skill development. It does not establish long-term career or labour-market effects.
qs: We are motivated by whether this productivity comes from free or at a cost.

These three patterns of interaction with AI, which resulted in higher scores in our skill evaluation, involve more cognitive effort and independent thinking (for example, asking for explanations or asking conceptual questions only).

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts the distinction between assisted task performance and durable skill growth and materially strengthens it with randomized coding evidence: AI users scored 17% lower on subsequent skill evaluation without a statistically significant completion-time gain. It further develops the cluster’s verification concern by arguing that inhibited learning may weaken users’ later ability to validate and debug AI-generated code, while limiting this inference to a short-term experimental setting.
qs: We find that using AI assistance to complete tasks that involve this new library resulted in a reduction in the evaluation score by 17% or two grade points (Cohen’s d = 0.738, p = 0.010).

This suggests that as companies transition to more AI code writing with human supervision, humans may not possess the necessary skills to validate and debug AI-written code if their skill formation was inhibited by using AI in the first place.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core competence-risk proposition and materially strengthens it with randomized evidence that AI assistance can impair skill formation without significant average efficiency gains. It also links cognitively engaged use to better learning and warns that weakened expertise may undermine later verification, while appropriately limiting generalization from a short programming study to legal practice.
qs: We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without                                                delivering significant efficiency gains on average.

Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a                                                shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill                                                formation – particularly in safety-critical domains.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts that AI outcomes depend on the task and workflow, then materially extends the proposition by experimentally separating assisted task completion from skill formation. It shows that cognitively disengaged delegation can impair learning, while explanation-seeking and conceptual engagement can preserve it, making interaction strategy and independent thought key conditions for durable gains.
qs: We find that AI use impairs conceptual understanding, code reading, and debugging abilities, without                                                delivering significant efficiency gains on average.

Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a                                                shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill                                                formation – particularly in safety-critical domains.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-specific, human-led framing and materially extends it with randomized evidence that AI use can impair skill formation when users offload generation or debugging. It strengthens the cluster’s concern that work redesign must preserve cognitive engagement and professional development so future reviewers retain the expertise needed for meaningful verification, while appropriately limiting its evidence to a short programming experiment rather than legal work.
qs: 7     Discussion Our main finding is that using AI to complete tasks that require a new skill (i.e., knowledge of a new Python library) reduces skill formation.

This suggests that as companies transition to more AI code writing with human supervision, humans may not possess the necessary skills to validate and debug AI-written code if their skill formation was inhibited by using AI in the first place.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that practical AI effects must be measured across distinct outcomes rather than inferred from task completion or capability. Its randomized experiment found significantly weaker immediate skill formation without a conclusive speed effect, while its narrow, short-duration design limits claims about long-term deskilling or workplace productivity.
qs: 5.2.2   Results Figure 6 shows that while using AI to complete our coding task did not significantly improve task completion time, the level of skill formation gained by completing the task, measured by our quiz, is significantly reduced (Cohen d=0.738, p=0.01).
We measured skill formation for      a specific Python library over a one-hour period.

st.t: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between assisted task performance and durable competence: its randomized trial finds reduced formation of a new programming skill despite no significant overall efficiency gain. It also supports the cluster’s emphasis on interaction patterns and cognitive engagement, while its workplace-development warning remains an extrapolation rather than a measured long-term outcome.

While using AI improved the average completion time of the task, the improvement in efficiency was not significant in our study, despite the AI Assistant being able to generate the complete code solution when prompted.

kp.k: AI-assisted task completion can bypass professional skill acquisition
kp.d: The authors investigate software engineering as a setting where workers learn unfamiliar tools on the job. Their framework distinguishes completing a task from acquiring the knowledge needed to perform and supervise it. This is cross-domain evidence about professional formation, not a study of lawyers or legal services.
qs: We hypothesize that using AI tools to generate code in the development process effectively amounts to taking a shortcut to task completion without a pronounced learning stage.
We seek to understand both the impact of AI on productivity and skill formation.

kp.k: Randomized experiment tested learning an unfamiliar programming library
kp.d: The main study analyzed 52 participants, with 26 assigned to each condition, completing two Python Trio tasks within 35 minutes. Participants had more than one year of Python experience, used Python at least weekly, had previously tried AI coding assistance, and had never used Trio. The AI condition used a GPT-4o chat assistant capable of generating complete correct solutions; controls had instructions and web search. Subsequent unaided assessment comprised 14 questions worth 27 points covering conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging, rather than code writing.
qs: In our main study, 52 participants completed the task, 26 for each of the control and treatment groups.
The base model used for this assistant is GPT-4o, and the model is prompted to be an intelligent coding assistant.
The final evaluation we used contained 14 questions for a total of 27 points.
All participants were not allowed to use AI in the comprehension check.

kp.k: AI assistance significantly reduced immediate learning outcomes
kp.d: The authors report lower quiz performance with AI assistance: Cohen’s d=0.738, p=0.01, with a 4.15-point difference on the 27-point quiz, which the paper describes as a 17% score difference or two grade points. Adjusting for warm-up task time left the effect significant (d=0.725, p=0.016). Control-group average scores were higher across coding-experience groups. These results concern acquisition of unfamiliar library skills, not demonstrated deterioration of previously mastered skills.
qs: There is a 4.15 point difference between the means of the treatment and control groups.
For a 27-point quiz, this translates into a 17% score difference or 2 grade points.
Controlling for warm-up task time as a covariate, the treatment effect remains significant (Cohen’s d=0.725, p=0.016).
Across all levels of prior coding experience, users scored higher on average in the control (no AI) than in the treatment (AI assistance) group (Figure 7).

kp.k: Average speed improvement was not statistically significant
kp.d: The main study found no conclusive acceleration or slowdown, with Figure 6 reporting p=0.391 for task time. Nevertheless, all AI participants completed the second task, whereas four of 26 controls did not finish it within 35 minutes. The authors attribute the lack of significant average speed gains to heterogeneous interaction costs: some participants spent up to 11 minutes interacting with AI or asked as many as 15 questions. This differs from established-task productivity gains reported in prior research.
qs: Our results do not conclusively find a speed up or slow down using AI in this task.
4 of the 26 participants in the control (No AI) group did not complete the second task within the 35-minute limit, while every participant in the AI condition completed the second task.
Some participants in the treatment group spent significant time (up to 11 minutes) interacting with the AI Assistant.

kp.k: Heavy delegation correlated with poor learning
kp.d: Qualitative analysis identified three low-scoring patterns, each containing four participants: AI Delegation averaged 19.5 minutes and 39% on the quiz; Progressive AI Reliance averaged 22 minutes and 35%; Iterative AI Debugging averaged 31 minutes and 24%. Complete delegation was fastest, while repeated AI troubleshooting combined poor learning with slower completion. These small, behavior-defined clusters are observational comparisons within the treatment condition, not randomized tests of interaction strategies.
qs: Low-scoring patterns generally involved a heavy reliance on AI, either through code generation or debugging.
AI Delegation (n=4): Participants in this group wholly relied on AI to write code and complete the task.
Progressive AI Reliance (n=4): Participants in this group started by asking 1 or 2 questions and eventually delegated all code writing to the AI assistant.
This group made a higher number of queries to the AI assistant, but relied on the assistant to solve problems, rather than clarifying their own understanding.

kp.k: Cognitively engaged AI use preserved stronger learning
kp.d: Three higher-scoring patterns combined assistance with deliberate understanding: Generation-Then-Comprehension (n=2) averaged 24 minutes and 86%; Hybrid Code-Explanation (n=3) averaged 24 minutes and 68%; Conceptual Inquiry (n=7) averaged 22 minutes and 65%. Participants sought explanations after generation, requested explanations alongside code, or restricted AI to conceptual questions while independently implementing and debugging. The authors interpret these small clusters as evidence that cognitive engagement matters more than simply whether AI is used.
qs: High-scoring interaction patterns were clusters of behaviors where the average quiz score is 65% or higher.
After their code was generated, they then asked the AI assistant follow-up questions to improve understanding.
Participants in this group composed hybrid queries in which they asked for code generation along with explanations of the generated code.
Participants in this group only asked conceptual questions and relied on their improved understanding to complete the task.

kp.k: Independent error resolution may help build debugging competence
kp.d: Controls encountered a median of three errors versus one for AI users; among 12 participants encountering no errors, only two were controls. Controls also encountered more errors involving Trio-specific concepts. Exploratory, non-preregistered assessment breakdowns showed the largest score gap in debugging and the smallest in code reading. The authors propose independently encountering and resolving errors as a learning mechanism; this mechanism was not separately randomized.
qs: The AI group encountered fewer errors than the control group: the median participant in the treatment group encountered only one error in the entire task, while the median for the control group was three errors.
Among the different types of questions, the largest score gap occurs in the debugging questions and the smallest score gap in the code reading questions.
Together, these two differences suggest that encountering errors may play a significant role in the formation of coding skills.

kp.k: Debugging reliance mattered more than total query volume
kp.d: Explanation requests were most common (79 queries), followed by generation (51), debugging (9), capabilities questions (4) and appreciation (4); 11 queries received two labels. Of 25 treatment participants examined for query behavior, 21 asked explanation questions and 16 requested generation. A higher fraction of debugging queries correlated with longer completion time (r=0.43, p=0.033) and lower quiz scores (r=-0.41, p=0.043), while total query count showed no clear relationship with quiz performance.
qs: 21 out of 25 participants in the treatment group asked an explanation question; this reflects the high level of engagement among our participants.
Only 16 of 25 or two thirds of the participants used AI to generate code.
There is no clear pattern between the number of total queries and quiz score.
This suggests that relying on AI for debugging (e.g. repetatedly asking AI to check and fix things without understanding) when learning a new task is correlated with less learning.

kp.k: Manual copying did not substitute for conceptual engagement
kp.d: Directly pasting generated code produced the fastest completion, whereas manually copying or mixing copying and pasting produced speeds similar to controls. The authors found no notable quiz-score difference between typing and pasting AI output. AI also shifted activity away from active coding toward interaction and comprehension, suggesting that additional mechanical effort or elapsed time alone does not ensure learning.
qs: For skill formation, measured by quiz score, there was no notable difference between groups that typed vs directly pasted AI output.
This suggests that spending more time manually typing may not yield better conceptual understanding.
Cognitive effort may be more important than the raw time spent on completing the task.
Time spent coding shifted to time spent interacting with AI and understanding AI generations (Figure 16).

kp.k: Pilot findings depended partly on unrelated syntax barriers
kp.d: Pilot D (n=20) found faster AI-assisted completion (d=1.11, p=0.03) alongside worse quiz performance (d=1.7, p=0.003); completion rates were 90% with AI and 60% without it. Screen recordings showed controls struggling with Python syntax unrelated to Trio, so syntax hints were added before the main experiment. Earlier pilots also exposed substantial prohibited AI use, leading to a platform change and screen-recording checks. These refinements qualify comparisons between pilot and main-study productivity results.
qs: The task competition rate within the 35-minute time limit was only 60% within the control (no AI) group compared to a 90% completion rate in the treatment (AI) group.
Since our focus was not Python syntax, we added syntax hints about string formatting and try/except blocks for the main study.
Using screen recordings of participant progress, we verified that participants did not use AI in the control group nor for the quiz.

kp.k: AI made tasks feel easier without easing assessment
kp.d: Exploratory self-reports showed higher perceived learning among controls and high enjoyment in both conditions. AI users perceived the coding task as easier, but both groups found the subsequent quiz similarly challenging. Some AI participants retrospectively wished they had examined explanations or library details more carefully; these comments illustrate experiences rather than establishing general effects.
qs: The control group (No AI) reported higher self-reported learning (on a 7-point scale), while both groups reported high levels of enjoyment in completing the task (Figure 9).
although participants in the treatment group (AI Assistance) found the task easier than the control group, both groups found the post-task quiz similarly challenging.
By using the AI assistant, I feel like I got lazy.

kp.k: Human oversight depends on skills automation may inhibit
kp.d: The authors argue that engineers still need conceptual, reading and debugging competence to check AI-generated code before deployment. They warn that pressure to maximize short-term completion may impair juniors’ acquisition of those very oversight skills. This is a prospective organizational and safety implication drawn from the learning results, not measured evidence of workplace failures or legal-professional outcomes.
qs: This additional verification that enhances safety is only possible when human engineers themselves have the skills to understand code and identify errors.
Given time constraints and organizational pressures, junior developers or other professionals may rely on AI to complete tasks as fast as possible at the cost of real skill development.

This suggests that as companies transition to more AI code writing with human supervision, humans may not possess the necessary skills to validate and debug AI-written code if their skill formation was inhibited by using AI in the first place.

kp.k: Long-term and agentic effects remain untested
kp.d: The study measured unfamiliar-library learning over approximately one hour, not months or years of professional development. Participants lacked real-job incentives to master Trio; prompting fluency was not directly measured, evaluation used a quiz rather than a subsequent coding task, and there was no human-assistance comparison. The authors predict that agentic or autocomplete tools could exacerbate learning losses by reducing participation, but identify testing those systems and longitudinal workplace outcomes as future research.
qs: We measured skill formation for a specific Python library over a one-hour period.
While participants in our study were professional or freelance programmers, there was not the same incentive to learn the library as if it were required for their actual job.
We do not include the counterfactual of how skill formation would be impacted by receiving assistance from humans.
Future work should investigate the impacts of agentic coding tools on learning outcomes and skill development.

kp.k: Organizations should preserve intentional learning alongside AI productivity
kp.d: The authors recommend careful integration of AI into workflows, especially safety-critical ones, with attention to cognitive effort and sustained expertise rather than productivity alone. They note that AI can assist such effort through explanation-oriented interaction and available learning modes; the paper does not evaluate those commercial learning modes.
qs: Our findings suggest that AI-enhanced productivity is not a shortcut to competence and AI assistance should be carefully adopted into workflows to preserve skill formation – particularly in safety-critical domains.
Exerting cognitive effort can be assisted by AI; beyond the patterns we describe, major LLM services also provide learning modes (e.g., ChatGPT Study Mode, Claude Code Learning / Explanatory mode).
Participants in the new AI economy must care not only about productivity gains from AI but also the long-term sustainability of expertise development amid the proliferation of new AI tools.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shen and Tamkin find that AI-assisted completion of unfamiliar programming tasks reduces immediate skill formation without a statistically significant average improvement in completion time.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about software engineering, not an original study of legal services. The authors report reduced conceptual understanding, code reading and debugging proficiency after learning the Python Trio library with AI assistance. In the main randomized experiment, the reported quiz-score difference was 4.15 points on a 27-point quiz, described in the paper as a 17% difference or two grade points (Cohen’s d=0.738, p=0.010). The AI group completed tasks somewhat faster on average, but the completion-time effect was not significant (p=0.391). All AI participants completed the second task; four control participants did not finish it within the time limit. Thus, the authors distinguish successful task completion from acquisition of the underlying competence.

pts.k: The authors claim that how workers use AI matters: cognitive engagement can preserve learning, whereas delegation and reliance on AI debugging are associated with poorer learning.
pts.d: Their qualitative typology distinguishes three lower-scoring patterns—AI Delegation (39%, 19.5 minutes, n=4), Progressive AI Reliance (35%, 22 minutes, n=4), and Iterative AI Debugging (24%, 31 minutes, n=4)—from three higher-scoring patterns: Generation-Then-Comprehension (86%, 24 minutes, n=2), Hybrid Code-Explanation (68%, 24 minutes, n=3), and Conceptual Inquiry (65%, 22 minutes, n=7). These are observed behavioral clusters, not separately randomized interventions. The authors also report no notable learning difference between manually typing and directly pasting AI-generated code, arguing that cognitive effort matters more than copying mechanics or elapsed task time.

pts.k: The authors explain the productivity and learning results through interaction overhead and reduced opportunities to encounter and independently resolve errors.
pts.d: Some participants spent up to 11 minutes interacting with the assistant, offsetting potential time savings. AI participants encountered a median of one error, versus three in the control group. Control participants encountered more Trio-specific errors, which the authors suggest promoted understanding through independent problem-solving. The largest exploratory subarea score gap was in debugging. These proposed mechanisms draw on screen recordings and exploratory analyses rather than independent randomized tests of interaction time or error exposure.

pts.k: The authors warn that productivity-driven AI adoption may weaken the expertise needed for human verification, and predict potentially greater learning losses with agentic or autocomplete tools.
pts.d: Shen and Tamkin extrapolate from their experiment to professional development: organizational pressure to finish work quickly may encourage junior developers and other professionals to bypass learning. They warn that a transition from writing code to supervising AI-written code could leave workers without the skills to validate and debug outputs. They further suggest that agentic and autocomplete interfaces could worsen this problem by removing the cognitive work of composing queries. These are conditional implications and predictions; the study did not test long-term workplace development, actual oversight performance, or agentic tools.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central evidence is a preregistered randomized experiment with 52 participants, supplemented by pilots, a library-specific skills quiz, screen recordings and exploratory behavioral analysis.
pts.d: The main study assigned 26 participants per condition to two Trio coding tasks, with GPT-4o chat assistance available in the treatment condition. Both groups subsequently completed an unaided 14-question, 27-point quiz covering seven concepts through conceptual, code-reading and debugging questions; code-writing questions were excluded. The learning effect remained significant after controlling for warm-up task time (d=0.725, p=0.016). Pilot D (n=20) found both faster completion with AI (d=1.11, p=0.03) and poorer quiz performance (d=1.7, p=0.003); the researchers then added Python syntax hints to reduce barriers unrelated to Trio. Early pilots had substantial unauthorized AI use, prompting a platform change and screen-recording checks. The behavioral typology and proposed mechanisms are exploratory, with small clusters. Background claims about productivity gains, including legal question-answering, are attributed to prior literature rather than presented as new legal-domain findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The demonstrated effects concern immediate learning during a short, unfamiliar-library task; longer-term professional and agentic-tool effects remain untested.
pts.d: The February 2026 paper measures skill formation over approximately one hour, with up to 35 minutes for the two coding tasks and an immediate unaided quiz. Participants were instructed to work as quickly as possible and were paid a flat $150. The assistant could generate complete, correct solutions when prompted, but used a chat interface rather than executing the work autonomously. The authors acknowledge the narrow task setting, absence of real-job learning incentives, unmeasured prompting fluency, quiz-based evaluation and lack of a human-assistance comparison. They explicitly call for longitudinal research over months or years. The results concern acquisition of new library-specific skills, not demonstrated decay of previously mastered skills.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct subjects are Python developers learning an unfamiliar library; the authors’ broader concern is novice professionals and organizations depending on skilled human oversight.
pts.d: Participants had more than one year of Python experience, used Python at least weekly, had previously tried AI coding assistance, and had never used Trio. Most were professional or freelance developers, and most had at least four years of coding experience: novice status primarily concerns the new library, not necessarily entry-level employment. Control-group quiz averages were higher across coding-experience groups, but only four participants had one to three years of experience, limiting subgroup conclusions. The authors extend their warning to junior developers, other professionals acquiring skills on the job, and companies moving toward human supervision of AI-generated work, especially in safety-critical domains. The paper does not directly measure consequences for lawyers, law firms, legal clients or legal markets.
